newsitem.title: TURKEY: Greenaway beams ancient theme into multimedia age.
newsitem.headline: Greenaway beams ancient theme into multimedia age.

text.p: According to Peter Greenaway, we ain't seen nothing yet.

The British experimental film director, whose works people love or hate, sees the brink of the 21st century as the start of a new era in multimedia filmmaking for the post-Nintendo generation that dispenses with the old notion of storyline.
"I don't think we've seen any cinema yet," he enthuses. "All we've seen is a hundred years of illustrated text.
"(Steven) Spielberg, or Mike Leigh or (Wim) Wenders, you name any filmmaker anywhere in the world, first he has to have text before he can have an image."
So what should cinema be about, then?
"I sincerely believe cinema ought to be strongly image- conscious, it's the art of image-making," Greenaway told Reuters in Istanbul, where he was to judge the Istanbul film festival.

"It is the great 20th century art of extraordinary potential to go into thousands of different places, metaphorical and literal. We should utilise that, make magnificent cultural artefacts which express the new age we are moving into -- the information age, when we shall all become film directors." MULTIMEDIA "FILM-OPERA" AND NEW TECHNIQUES
A description of a Peter Greenaway "film-opera", written by himself and entitled "One Hundred New Objects to Represent the World", may give a clue about information-age films.

The opera, which will open the Salzburg Austrian opera festival this summer, employs 410 different pieces of film projected from 32 projectors to back three singers on stage, whose live singing intermingles with a synthesised and harmonised soundtrack of natural sounds, singing and speaking human voices, and is backed by a famous German percussionist.
The stage will be an installation, open to the public from 10 a.m. until the conductor steps out at 6 p.m.

In his latest film, "The Pillow Book", Greenaway experiments with video techniques, using multiple screens, and he plans to take things further by organising his next picture, "The Tulse Luper Suitcase", like a CD-Rom and putting it on the Internet.

Greenaway is impatient with current hits, such as nine- Oscar winner "The English Patient": "Why do people bother to make a film like The English Patient? What a waste of time! It existed perfectly well as a book, a very good book," he said.
"Cinema is not an adjunct of the bookshop round the corner ...I don't think cinema is a very good narrative medium, if you want to tell stories become a writer, don't become a filmmaker."
THE ONLY SUBJECT MATTERS ARE SEX AND DEATH
For all the technological innovations, Greenaway does not plan to change the subject matter of his films, which deal with grotesque and extreme behaviour in sumptuous surroundings.

"There are only two subject matters -- one is sex and the other is death. That is not original, that is the condition of Western art," he said. "(Honore de) Balzac, the French writer, suggested there was a third subject matter and it was money, but money can easily be subsumed into sex and death -- you earn money to get one and deprive yourself of the other."
From his first feature film in 1982, "The Draughtsman's Contract", Greenaway has shocked and confronted people with the consequences of the voyeurism now pervasive in popular culture.

"I think that it is a characteristic of the 20th century that we are all interested in sex and violence and sensation," he said. "And I think in some sense if that is the current language, we shouldn't run away and hide."

His examination engendered violent and witty acts of revenge such as a husband having his wife's bookish lover fed to death with books in "The Cook, the Thief, his Wife and her Lover", and his wife making him eat the lover he killed in the same film.
In his 1993 feature film, "The Baby of Macon", which stars Ralph Fiennes, he shows gang rape and child mutilation, and includes an 11-minute rape scene involving 202 men.
Greenaway says his films are the continuation of a tradition that goes back to Shakespeare.
"People had their hands chopped off, women were humiliated -- these are extremes of human behaviour which is a tradition that has been followed by a lot of European drama," he said.
"If we examine the extremes of human behaviour we'll be able to understand where most of us reside for most of the time."
HAPPY ACCIDENT THAT CREATED A FILMMAKER
Greenaway, 54, is also a painter and says his interest in the cinema was born of a "happy accident" at art school.

"One very wet afternoon the fat boy in the class suggested that since we couldn't play cricket because it was raining we should go down to the local flea pit," he said, referring to seedy local cinemas where in the 1960s managers showed Swedish films because of their soft pornographic content.
But by luck more than design, the manager of that cinema happened to show Ingmar Bergman's 'The Seventh Seal'.

"Here was a film which was deeply, deeply serious and it had a tremendous, profound effect on me. And I suppose at that particular moment I thought "Ah, that is what I want to do. I want to make things like that," Greenaway said.
Greenaway has no illusions that he is anything but a marginal director in Britain: "I always comfort myself that there are always more people abroad than there are at home."
HOLLYWOOD A "NECESSARY EVIL"
He is pragmatic about Hollywood, which he predicts will die off like the dinosours but remains a necessary evil now.

"I can't keep a cinema open, it is impossible...My movies occupy a very, very small space of cinema time," he said. "So we have to have somebody who looks after the cinemas of the world while they are waiting for my film to appear."
